title: ICF systems sold in Ontario, compared | GTA ICF
description: Nudura, Amvic, Logix, Fox Blocks, BuildBlock, Quad-Lock, Plasti-Fab, Polycrete and Nexcem side by side on the makers' own published figures, with sources.
h1: ICF systems sold in Ontario, compared
lede: A homeowner or builder in southern Ontario will be offered one of about nine insulated concrete form systems, usually whichever one the nearest yard stocks. This guide is for anyone holding two quotes that name different forms. It ranks nothing and recommends nothing: we install whichever system the local supplier carries, so we have no favourite. What it does is put the manufacturers' own published figures side by side, core widths, foam per face, the R-value each maker prints and on what basis, the listing behind it and where it is made, so you can see where two quotes actually differ.

sections.heading: Why the brand matters less than people think
paragraphs: Ontario's Building Code does not name an ICF brand. Article 9.15.4.1 asks every flat wall ICF unit to conform to CAN/ULC-S717.1, the material standard for the forms, and that is the only product requirement it makes. The structural rules are about the concrete inside the foam. Sentence 9.15.4.2.(2) sets a foundation core of not less than 150 mm (6 in), and never thinner than the concrete in the wall above. Article 9.20.17.1 sets an above-ground core of not less than 140 mm, constant for the full height. Every system whose sizes we could retrieve offers a 6 in core or larger, so the Code's minimum is met by all of them.

Energy works the same way. SB-12 deems an ICF wall with at least RSI 1.76 (R10) of insulation on each face of the concrete to comply with the wall values in Table 3.1.1.2.A, and allows it in place of basement walls that need RSI 3.52 ci (R20) or less. That test is about the foam on each face of the chosen form, not the name on the pallet. Nominal means the foam alone; the effective value for the whole wall is what the SB-12 tables use, and it comes from the manufacturer's thermal report for the block on your quote. Reviewers may ask for that product literature with the SB-12 submission.

Then there is the paperwork. The Code asks for S717.1 conformance, not a CCMC number. The NRC's registry lists two ICF systems under CAN/ULC-S717.1, Amvic (13043-L) and Plasti-Fab's Advantage (13101-L), plus one code-compliance report, for Polycrete (13354-R). Nudura, Logix, Fox Blocks, BuildBlock and Quad-Lock do not appear there; they hold S717.1 listings or certifications from Intertek or QAI, which are also accredited bodies. Quad-Lock's compliance page says plainly that no CCMC report is required for an acceptable solution referenced in the codes. Whichever system is on your quote, its listing document goes in the permit package, and we prepare that package with you.

sections.heading: The systems side by side
paragraphs: Every cell below comes from the manufacturer's own website, data sheet or listing document, or from the NRC registry, and the source list under the table names each one. Where a manufacturer does not print a figure on the pages we read, the cell says so rather than guessing. Two suppliers' sites would not load for our tools: Polycrete's returned an access error or an empty page, so its row is built from its CCMC report, and Plasti-Fab's current site no longer lists the Advantage ICF System at all, so its row carries the listing and the plants and nothing else. Logix Brands now also sells under the Element ICF name, and its QAI listing covers both.

Read the R column with care. Amvic prints R22 and R30 for completed walls with 2.5 in and 3.25 in panels. Quad-Lock's figures include R-2.66 for air films, drywall, concrete and a wood finish, so they are closer to a whole-assembly number. Nudura and Logix print the foam's resistance per inch and leave the wall figure to their design documents. Fox Blocks prints 23.5 plus. None of these is the effective value the SB-12 tables use; that comes from the third-party thermal report for the block. Core widths are nominal, and Logix's 6.25 in is its own standard size rather than a misprint.

sections.heading: What actually differs between systems on site
paragraphs: The differences a crew feels are not in the R column. The first is web spacing, because the web flanges are what drywall and cladding screw into. Amvic's R22 block and BuildBlock put webs at 6 in on centre; Nudura, Logix and Amvic's R30 use 8 in; Quad-Lock ties sit on a 12 in grid; Element Chrome has side webs at 16 in with loose Flexties between them. Nudura's flange is 1 1/2 in (38 mm) wide and recessed 1/2 in below the foam, and BuildBlock and Element Chrome print the same width and recess. Tighter spacing gives the finisher more to hit and, BuildBlock argues, less bulging of the foam under concrete pressure.

The second is the unit itself. A Nudura form is 96 in long and 18 in high; most others are 48 by 16 in; Quad-Lock is a 48 by 12 in panel assembled with ties; Polycrete's Big Block is 2 440 mm long and up to 610 mm high; Nexcem units are 12 in high and 24 or 36 in long. Height sets the coursing, so a wall height that stacks cleanly in 16 in courses may need a cut course in 18 in, and the reverse. Nudura's own design page says to put any partial course at the footing or the top, not mid-wall, and to cut panels at 9 in or less so the offcut is reusable.

The third is the accessory catalogue. Every EPS system here sells 90 degree corners; Amvic, Nudura, Logix and BuildBlock also sell 45s, and BuildBlock's corner legs are 6 in longer than what it calls the industry standard. Taper-top forms, which widen the core at the top of a wall for a floor or roof bearing, come from Amvic, Fox Blocks, Logix and Polycrete; brick-ledge forms from those four plus Nudura, with Quad-Lock using a brick-ledge tie instead. Bracing is a separate purchase or rental for all of them: Amvic's site lists Plumwall, BuildBlock sells BuildBrace and lists Zont and Zuckle, and Quad-Lock's corner brackets are meant to remove the bracing at corners.

sections.heading: How to compare quotes from two suppliers
paragraphs: Start by making the two quotes describe the same wall. Both should name the system and the model, the core width, the EPS thickness per face, the block count, and which special forms are included. If one quote is priced on a 6 in core and the other on 8 in, or one includes corners, taper tops and bracing rental and the other does not, the totals are not comparable. Check the core against the drawings, not against habit: the Code minimum is 150 mm below grade and 140 mm above, and an engineer's or designer's specification can ask for more.

Then ask each supplier for two documents: the listing to CAN/ULC-S717.1 or the CCMC evaluation for that exact product, and the thermal report that gives the effective value SB-12 uses. Compare the per-face insulation with SB-12's RSI 1.76 (R10) each side. Ask what the yard has in stock in your core width, its lead time, and whether the corners and taper tops ship from the same place. Ask about the warranty in writing: Nudura publishes a 30-year limited warranty on minimum thermal resistance and acoustic performance from the date of delivery; the others we checked either point to a warranty document or print nothing, so ask.

Price last. Our own figures are illustrative ranges per square foot of wall from our price table, firm price after a site review, and they sit in the ICF against poured guide rather than here. What a comparison between two forms will show is small: block cost is one line inside a wall price that is mostly concrete, steel, labour, pump time and waterproofing. A cheaper block that needs a cut course every lift, or that arrives a week late, costs more than the difference. We say which system a quote is priced on, and we will re-price on the other if you ask.
list: Which system and model, which core width and which EPS thickness per face, in writing on the quote.
The S717.1 listing number or CCMC number for that product, and the thermal report behind the printed R-value.
Block height, so the wall stacks without a cut course, and the offcut plan if it cannot.
Which special forms are included: corners, taper tops, brick ledges, bucks, and who provides the bracing.
Stock in your core width at the local yard, the lead time, and the delivery date in the contract.
The manufacturer's warranty terms and how a claim is made.

sections.heading: Nexcem: a cement-bonded wood-fibre form
paragraphs: Nexcem belongs in its own section because it is a different material. Its units are cement-bonded wood fibre, with no polystyrene and no plastic webs; the manufacturer calls them ICCF, insulated composite concrete forms, and says the base unit's material alone gives R-8 to R-12. The catalogue runs from a 6 in unit with a 3.2 in core to 16 in units with a 12.5 in core, all 12 in high and 24 or 36 in long. Insulation inserts of 1.5 to 7 in raise the published total to R-14, R-22, R-28 or R-36 while narrowing the core. Basement walls, it says, typically need at least a 6.5 in core.

The compliance route is different too. CAN/ULC-S717.1, as Quad-Lock's technical page quotes its scope, is written for modular expanded polystyrene units connected by cross ties, and the Code's Part 9 ICF articles hang on that standard. A wood-fibre unit is not that product, so expect the wall to be designed rather than read from the Part 9 tables; Nexcem itself points designers to reinforced concrete design to CSA A23.3 based on the core. We could not load Nexcem's approvals page, so we print no listing for it: ask the company what document it provides for an Ontario permit. Its own cost page puts the block above polystyrene ICF on a materials-only basis.

sections.heading: Where a particular system is the wrong choice
paragraphs: The wrong system is usually the right system in the wrong place. If the engineer has specified a 10 in core for a tall walk-out wall, Amvic's R30 line stops at 8 in and Element Chrome starts at 6 in, so the quote has to move to a line that carries the size. Logix's 6.25 in standard is fine against a 150 mm minimum, but the concrete order and the footing width should be figured on 159 mm, not 152. If the yard nearest the site cannot deliver corners and taper tops with the straights, a system with a better form on paper becomes a stalled wall on the day.

Thin panels need a second look under SB-12. Quad-Lock's 2 1/4 in Regular panel is one the manufacturer itself recommends only for experienced installers, and its published R-values are built from panel combinations rather than a fixed per-face thickness. Before the SB-12 form is filled in, the per-face value has to be read from the manufacturer's sheet against the RSI 1.76 (R10) each side that the deemed-to-comply sentence asks for. Plasti-Fab's Advantage system still holds an active CCMC listing, but the company's current site does not list it among its products, so confirm it is stocked before a quote is written on it.

And there are jobs where no ICF system is the better choice. A wall over 3 m floor to floor, soil under 75 kPa, or a plan with many jogs and wide openings leaves the Part 9 tables and goes to Part 4 whatever the brand. There, a poured and insulated wall or a simpler plan is often quicker to review, and we say so at the site review, not after the permit is in. Polycrete's CCMC report is a narrower case: it is tied to the Trois-Rivières plant, to NBC 2015 and to the company's own installation manual, and those conditions travel with it into an Ontario permit package.

faqs.a: None of them, in the sense the question means. Ontario's Building Code asks for a flat wall form that conforms to CAN/ULC-S717.1 and a concrete core of at least 150 mm below grade, and every system in our table whose sizes we could retrieve meets both. What differs is web spacing, block height, the special forms in the catalogue, the panel thickness, and which yard near you stocks it. We install whichever system the local supplier carries, and the quote names it.

faqs.q: Nudura vs Amvic vs Logix: what is the actual difference?
faqs.a: Nudura is a 96 by 18 in form with 2 5/8 in panels and webs at 8 in, with a Toronto manufacturer address and licensee plants. Amvic's R22 is 48 by 16 in with 2.5 in panels and webs at 6 in, its R30 has 3.25 in panels, and it holds CCMC 13043-L. Logix, now also sold as Element ICF, is 48 by 16 in with 2 3/4 in panels, webs at 8 in, a 6.25 in standard core and a plant in Cobourg. All three list to S717.1.

faqs.q: Does the ICF brand matter for the building permit?
faqs.a: Not in the Code. Article 9.15.4.1 asks for conformance to CAN/ULC-S717.1, and none of the municipal websites we checked publishes an ICF-specific checklist. What matters is that the system on the drawings is the system on site, and that its listing or CCMC document and its thermal data are in the package if the reviewer asks. Only Amvic, Plasti-Fab's Advantage and Polycrete appear on the NRC's registry; the others hold Intertek or QAI listings.

faqs.q: Can two ICF brands be mixed on one job?
faqs.a: Mixing accessories is normal; mixing forms in one wall is not. Bucks, bracing and connectors are sold as brand-neutral: Amvic's AmBuck is described as compatible with 6 and 8 in core ICF systems, and both Amvic and BuildBlock list third-party bracing. The forms themselves have different heights and interlocks, 18 in against 16 in against 12 in panels, and each listing and installation manual covers its own product. One system per wall, named on the quote, keeps the permit package clean.

faqs.q: What should I ask an ICF supplier before I sign?
faqs.a: Six things. The system and model, core width and EPS thickness per face, in writing. The S717.1 listing number or CCMC number for that product. The thermal report behind the printed R-value, since SB-12 wants RSI 1.76 (R10) on each face. Stock in your core width at the local yard and the lead time. Which corners, taper tops, brick ledges and bracing are included. And the warranty terms, because they range from Nudura's published 30 years to nothing printed at all.

faqs.q: Which ICF systems are made in Ontario?
faqs.a: By the manufacturers' own documents: Nudura's specification gives a Toronto manufacturer address, with licensee plants in Quebec, Alberta and Georgia. The QAI evaluation report for Logix and Element ICF lists a plant in Cobourg, Ontario among six. Plasti-Fab has plants in Ajax and Kitchener, though its site no longer lists the Advantage ICF. Nexcem gives a 647 number and Ontario projects but prints no plant address on the pages we read. Amvic, Fox Blocks, BuildBlock and Quad-Lock do not print an Ontario plant.

cta.heading: Send us both quotes and the drawings
cta.body: Email the two quotes, the plans and any engineer's notes. We will tell you whether the two forms are priced on the same wall, which core and EPS thickness the drawings need, and what to ask each yard, then give you a written quote after a site review.
